reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A mucinosis characterised by diffuse, symmetrical, non-pitting woody induration of the skin, typically beginning on the posterior neck, upper back and shoulders

Three clinical types are recognised: a post-infectious form (often after streptococcal or viral upper respiratory infection) that tends to resolve, a form associated with monoclonal gammopathy, and scleroedema diabeticorum linked to long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes
The skin over the upper trunk becomes thickened and bound down, sometimes with an orange-peel appearance and reduced ability to pinch or wrinkle the skin
The hands and feet are characteristically spared, helping to distinguish it from systemic sclerosis, and Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly are absent
Extensive disease can restrict movement of the neck, back and chest wall, and rarely involves the tongue, pharynx or heart
Histology shows a thickened reticular dermis with collagen bundles separated by mucin, producing characteristic fenestration, best demonstrated with colloidal iron or Alcian blue
Treatment is often unsatisfactory; phototherapy (particularly UVA1 or PUVA), optimisation of glycaemic control and physiotherapy are used, and the post-infectious form may resolve spontaneously
reference.pathophysiology: Scleroedema is a primary cutaneous mucinosis in which fibroblasts deposit excess collagen and glycosaminoglycans, chiefly hyaluronic acid, throughout a markedly thickened reticular dermis. In the post-infectious form, an immune response to preceding infection is thought to stimulate fibroblast activity transiently. In the diabetes-associated form, chronic hyperglycaemia is believed to promote non-enzymatic glycation of collagen, increase resistance to degradation and stimulate mucin production, accounting for its persistence. The paraproteinaemic form is associated with a monoclonal gammopathy that, as in scleromyxoedema, may drive fibroblast stimulation, although the mechanism is incompletely defined.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy from involved back or neck showing dermal thickening with mucin between collagen bundles
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin to assess for diabetes
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein
Antistreptolysin O titre and infection history in the post-infectious form
Thyroid function tests to exclude myxoedema
Assessment of chest wall and joint mobility where induration is extensive
redFlags: Restriction of chest wall movement causing respiratory compromise
Dysphagia or airway symptoms from pharyngeal or tongue involvement
Rapidly progressive induration or associated systemic symptoms prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: The post-infectious form usually resolves over months to a couple of years, whereas the diabetes-associated and paraprotein-related forms tend to be chronic and persistent. Serious systemic complications are uncommon, and prognosis is largely determined by the underlying association and the extent of functional restriction.
pitfalls: Confusing scleroedema with systemic sclerosis, despite the sparing of the hands and absence of Raynaud phenomenon
Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy requiring monitoring
Failing to distinguish the self-limiting post-infectious form from the persistent diabetic form when advising on prognosis
Taking a superficial biopsy that misses the deep dermal mucin and collagen changes
Neglecting glycaemic optimisation and physiotherapy in the diabetic form
management: Treat the underlying association: optimise glycaemic control in scleroedema diabeticorum and address any monoclonal gammopathy
Manage the post-infectious form expectantly as it usually resolves spontaneously, treating any residual streptococcal infection
Offer physiotherapy and stretching to preserve neck, back, and chest-wall mobility where induration is extensive
Consider phototherapy (PUVA or UVA1) or immunomodulation such as methotrexate, systemic corticosteroids, or intravenous immunoglobulin for progressive or disabling disease
Monitor for restrictive complications including chest-wall, cardiac, tongue, and pharyngeal involvement
Refer to dermatology, with haematology input where a paraprotein is identified
